newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. sees no improvement in human rights in Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sees no improvement in human rights in Iraq.

text.p: Iraqi journalists regarded as not following the government's line are reportedly sent to camps and subjected to degrading treatment such as having half their heads or moustaches shaved or one or two teeth pulled out, according to a U.N. report on Thursday.

"Another journalist was said to have been sentenced to life imprisonment for telling a joke about the president," said the report by U.N. human rights investigator Max van der Stoel, a former Netherlands foreign minister. His findings were based on information from Iraqi citizens who had recently arrived in Jordan and on other allegations received by the U.N. Centre for Human Rights.

On the overall situation, he said, "it remains clear that there has been no improvement in the situation of human rights in the country. It also remains clear that a small number of persons continue to be responsible for the tremendous suffering of the population."

Several decrees prescribing amputation for ordinary criminal offences continued to be in force in clear violation of international standards prohibiting such cruel, unusual and inhuman punishments, van der Stoel said.

Referring to military involvement beginning in late August in an inter-Kurdish conflict in northern Iraq, he said it was "evident that the imposition of military forces composed of tens of thousands of troops and including heavy artillery and tanks in action against civilian targets and resulting in numerous deaths and a large number of arrests and missing persons constitutes a clear violation of Security Council resolution 688 (1991)."
The resolution demanded that Iraq cease oppressing civilians, particularly in the northern Kurdish area.

Arbitrary arrests "were said still to be common throughout the country," with insecurity "substantially heightened by the usual treatment" that followed, van der Stoel said. "Upon arrest, cruel torture and gross mistreatment still occur. Several witnesses gave testimony about terrible tortures that they suffered, sometimes over long periods of time."

Referring to the government's grip on all means of mass communication, he quoted one witness as saying that in 1993 a telephone operator who warned a person not to call abroad because the lines were bugged was later "arrested, taken to his place of work and executed in front of his colleagues."

He said journalists, who were under pressure to join the ruling Baath party, "must obey orders when told what to write, especially instructions coming from the president's son, Uday. Those perceived as not obeying the official line are reportedly sent to camps and subjected to degrading treatment such as the shaving of one half of their moustache, shaving of their hair on only one side of the head or pulling out of one or two teeth."

He said when two elderly, very well-known journalists took the floor during a conference in Baghdad, Uday, accompanied by friends, "were said to have started to pelt them with tomatoes since they were perceived as not following his orders."

"They were subsequently beaten by the army and forbidden from exercising any activities having to do with the press. This was meant to serve as a deterrent for other journalists who were present at the meeting and witnessed the whole scene."
